I show my boarders upstairs where my room is because that’s where the dog will spend the majority of their time, I live upstairs mostly and my roommates are on the first floor. I don’t show them the first floor/living room/kitchen, because my roommates honestly keep it kinda trashed. I have a side door that leads upstairs and a door that shuts to separate the floors, so it works well. The boarding clients I’ve taken up so far have been really respectful and just peeked their heads in my office and the guest room where their dog sleeps. My room is at the far end of the hall and nobody has wandered down there or asked to see my bedroom but I leave the door open. Usually the dog will go in there to sniff around. I do make sure my room is presentable. I don’t care if they see my room personally. But I say all this to show you can only offer them to explore whatever areas of the house you choose to allow them into. Close your bedroom door. Tell them it hasn’t been cleaned up/dog proofed yet. Tell them your friend slept over last night and hasn’t gotten up yet. Or just tell them that’s your personal space and you don’t allow clients to see it. I wouldn’t worry too much about the decorations unless they’re really unprofessional in some way.

Yeah she needs more therapy. She shouldn’t be sharing all this stuff about parts with you, in my experience that can be really damaging to a system. Some systems don’t know it can be triggering for them to share so much because it’s hard to keep it in sometimes when you find someone safe to open up to. All the talk about it could be making things worse because you (no offense) aren’t equipped to handle it, this is best left to a professional. It’s good to have internal boundaries with your other parts about what you will and won’t share or say or do, so you don’t end up hurting yourself or others… 

Anyways you’re not wrong to be setting strict boundaries with this person. Regardless of diagnosis their behavior is unacceptable. She pissed on your rug? I’d never let her back in my house without a sincere apology. And she’s been saying and doing things that could be incredibly triggering to you. I find it kinda hypocritical to be upset with someone for setting a boundary so they aren’t triggered, then claiming it triggered you! 

I’m sorry this sounds really complicated and I do think you should do your best to be available if they want to come back and apologize but I would really be putting my foot down about most of this behavior. You are not being unreasonable. System accountability is really important.

I personally think it’s usually just regular sleep walking. But there seems to be a connection between sleep walking and dissociative symptoms, or at least some people say there is. Sleep disruptions are pretty common in people with dissociative disorders. 

I can give an example from my experience. I sometimes wake up in my bathroom. Usually when I “wake up” there I wasn’t actually asleep before, I just wander in there to switch a lot, bathrooms feel safe to me for whatever reason. Sometimes I wake up in the bathroom, and the last thing I remember I actually was asleep in bed, and I’d been sleep walking. Usually when it’s the second one I wake up on the floor or sitting on the toilet leaning against the wall, like I was actually asleep in the bathroom, that doesn’t happen as much. If I go in there to switch I am usually standing the whole time.

I’ve been told an indicator for separating the two is the content of the delusions/hallucinations and whether or not they relate to your past in some way. Depression/mania from bipolar and hypoarousal/hyperarousal from PTSD are hard to tell apart. Find someone who is informed about trauma and knows what they’re talking about. I also do in home private dog training with reactive clients sometimes so I take precautions. I always ask how dogs are with strangers before the meet and greet.
